summary: Field Shift is a decision-support web app that helps dryland farmers choose crop rotations that are more resilient to a changing climate, balancing profit, water use, and soil health, using NASA Earth-observation data alongside agricultural records. Rather than recommending a single crop for a single season, it compares a farmer’s current rotation against alternative multi-year rotations and scores each on the four things a farmer actually weighs: income, income in a bad year, how much of the crops’ water need is met by rainfall, and long-term soil health. The farmer sets how much each priority matters to them, and the ranking updates in response. This addresses the Field Shift challenge directly, which calls for a tool that combines NASA observations with local agricultural information to help farmers explore rotation strategies that strengthen soil health and adapt to shifting temperature, rainfall, and water conditions. It matters because the traditional wheat–fallow system common in dry regions leaves fields bare for 15 of every 24 months, and 65 to 80 percent of the rain that falls during fallow is lost to evaporation before a crop can use it. At the same time farmland itself is vanishing: in my home province of Ontario, 319 acres disappear to development every day. Helping farmers make the most of the land they already have is therefore both an economic and a food-security problem, and it is the problem Field Shift is built to help with.
details: For a chosen county, Field Shift shows the farmer’s current rotation beside the two best-fitting alternatives out of eight. Each option displays a month-by-month planting calendar, income in a normal and a bad year, the share of crop water need met by rainfall in typical and dry years, a soil-care score, and the number of months the field sits idle. Alongside the numbers it gives a plain-language explanation of why that rotation was suggested, and an expandable panel with the supporting evidence, the benefits, the information gaps, and the risks that would need review by a local agronomist. The same recommendation is also generated as a text-message mock-up, so it can reach farmers who do not have reliable data access. Under the hood, income and bad-year income come from a per-crop yield regression (a county effect, a technology trend, growing-season rainfall, and the number of days above 35 °C), which is then run through a Monte Carlo simulation of roughly 4,000 draws resampling past seasons; margin is yield times expected price minus operating cost, summed across the rotation and divided by the cycle length, and reported as a median and a bad-year (tenth-percentile) figure. The water score replays each rotation through the NASA monthly rainfall record from every possible start year, crediting a crop with the rain that falls while it grows plus a quarter of the rain on the idle months before it, measured against FAO reference crop-water needs. The soil-care score is a heuristic index built from the share of months with living roots, the diversity of crops, whether a nitrogen-fixing legume is present, and how much residue each crop leaves. To check that the engine is sound, a walk-forward backtest over 2012 to 2025 and 107 county-seasons returned 169 dollars per acre against 152 for simply chasing last year’s most profitable crop, a 10.6 percent improvement, with every decision made using only data from earlier years. The benefit of this approach is that it is evidence-based rather than rule-of-thumb, it shows ranges and trade-offs instead of false-precision single numbers, it is honest about its own data gaps, and because it runs entirely on free data it can be extended to any region. What I hope to achieve is to give farmers and the extension agents who advise them a credible starting point for choosing rotations that keep soil covered, use water efficiently, and still pay, and in doing so to reduce the water wasted on bare fallow ground. The project was built in Python, using pandas, NumPy, and statsmodels for the data and modelling, Streamlit for the dashboard, DuckDB for storage, Plotly for the charts, and the requests library for the API pulls. The pitch video and its graphics were produced with Pillow, Playwright with Chromium, FFmpeg, and the global-land-mask library, with Inter and Space Grotesk as the typefaces. Anthropic’s Claude was used as a coding and design assistant throughout. As next steps, the most important is to validate the rotation water and soil scores against published field-trial results, since those scores currently rest on general agronomy references rather than local measurement. Beyond that, I would add more regions and test cases, such as Maharashtra in India, the Rift Valley in Kenya, and Ontario in Canada, each with its own local yield and price data; expand the set of crops and cover-crop species; and account for effects the current model ignores, including the influence of the previous crop, tillage, irrigation, and crop insurance. I would also bring in more NASA datasets, using SMAP soil moisture to replace the fixed fallow-storage assumption, ECOSTRESS evapotranspiration to replace the FAO constants, MODIS and Landsat vegetation indices to measure planting as it actually happens, and GRACE and GRACE-FO to track groundwater, along with SSURGO soil and SRTM slope data for field-level erosion risk. Finally, I would build out real delivery through live SMS and WhatsApp in partnership with extension agents and co-ops.
